source_unit.exact_text: Evaluate small tails without subtractive cancellation. Use $Q(z)=\tfrac12\operatorname{erfc}(z/\sqrt2)$, where $\operatorname{erfc}(u)=\tfrac{2}{\sqrt\pi}\int_u^\infty e^{-s^2}\,ds$. The substitution $r=\sqrt2s$ in the normal-tail integral yields this identity. In floating-point arithmetic, $\Phi(z)$ may round to $1$ for large positive $z$, so $1-\Phi(z)$ can become a false zero. Direct upper-tail evaluation avoids that subtraction, though sufficiently extreme tails can still underflow and require stronger numerical methods. For $\sigma\gt0$ every true finite-threshold Gaussian tail is strictly positive; a displayed rounded zero cannot certify a zero cost budget. “Exact expectation” refers to the analytical formula, whose numerical evaluation still has rounding error.

claims.statement_in_prose: erfc(u)=2/sqrt(pi) times the genuine improper integral from u to infinity of exp(-s^2).
actual_hypotheses: u is any real; exp(-s^2) is integrable on the real line and the half-line.
claims.correspondence_assessment: erfc is defined by the actual Ioi set integral. The theorem proves IntegrableOn and the atTop limit of finite interval integrals, so the improper-integral notation is justified and not a bare renaming of a target probability.

claims.statement_in_prose: Q(z)=1/2 erfc(z/sqrt(2)); the substitution r=sqrt(2)*s produces this identity.
actual_hypotheses: z is real; sqrt(2)>0; true Gaussian normalization and density integral.
claims.correspondence_assessment: The actual integral change-of-variable theorem, square-root identity, transformed lower endpoint and Jacobian factor are all present in the proof body. The normalized density integral is the actual standard Gaussian upper-tail probability. No new mathematical implication is missing here.

claims.statement_in_prose: A finite-arithmetic CDF may round to one while the true Gaussian upper tail remains positive, causing a computed zero in 1-Phi.
actual_hypotheses: Actual standard Gaussian CDF and strict upper tail.
Nearest rounding to the explicitly decoded finite binary64 value set in [0,1].
For the conditional theorem Q(z)<2^-54; the eventual theorem derives this at all sufficiently large real thresholds.
claims.correspondence_assessment: The finite value set and nearest minimizer are constructed, not postulated. Every representable y<1 is at most 1-2^-53; the open upper rounding cell therefore maps to one. Gaussian-tail decay follows from the actual probability CDF limit. Strict positivity holds at every finite real threshold. Rounded subtraction maps 1-1 to representable zero. No roundedCDF=1 premise supplies the conclusion.

claims.statement_in_prose: Use the direct upper-tail expression to avoid subtracting a near-one CDF from one.
actual_hypotheses: Direct evaluation means rounding the exact real Q(z), equivalently the analytic erfc expression, once.
No guarantee is asserted for the reader JavaScript approximation or an arbitrary erfc implementation.
claims.correspondence_assessment: Continuity and the intermediate value theorem produce a finite nonnegative threshold with Q(z)=2^-60. An explicit exponent/fraction encoding represents that value, so direct rounding fixes it. CDF subtraction returns zero at the same threshold. This supplies a mathematical example supporting the advice, not a universal software error bound.

claims.statement_in_prose: Even a direct upper-tail evaluation can underflow for sufficiently extreme tails.
actual_hypotheses: The same nearest value model, with gradual subnormal values and minimum positive value 2^-1074.
All thresholds in the conclusion are finite real values; ties are excluded by strict inequalities.
claims.correspondence_assessment: The exponent/fraction bounds prove that every positive representable value is at least 2^-1074, and that this floor is attained. Below half that floor the nearest result is zero. The actual Gaussian tail tends to zero but remains positive at every finite threshold, so all sufficiently large thresholds give a positive true tail and a rounded zero, also for the equal real erfc expression.

claims.statement_in_prose: For nonzero noise, every monitored positive-time finite-threshold true Gaussian tail is positive.
actual_hypotheses: sigma>0 in the source is sufficient for sigma!=0; monitored times are >=1; thresholds are real.
claims.correspondence_assessment: Actual Gaussian measures are mutually absolutely continuous with volume at nonzero variance, making every finite strict upper half-line have positive mass. Finite AR probabilities are proved positive. The infinite marginal law gives the same positivity after a direct source bridge. This claim does not include deterministic time zero.

claims.statement_in_prose: A displayed rounded zero cannot certify a true zero expected unsafe-count budget when sigma>0 and T>0.
actual_hypotheses: The existing arbitrary-parameter positivity theorem covers sigma!=0 and T>0 on the original infinite noise space.
The new nonvacuous counterexample uses k=1/2, sigma=1, T=1 and a constructed real goal; 0<k<2 and sigma>0 hold.
The computed count is the printed sum of rounded CDF tail terms; T=1 requires no additional model of summation error.
claims.correspondence_assessment: The one-step mean, variance and standardized threshold are proved for the literal recurrence parameters. The actual infinite-path expected violation count equals Q(z), not an assigned surrogate. At the constructed threshold its true expectation is 2^-60>0, while the rounded CDF evaluation of that same count is zero and direct evaluation retains 2^-60. No claim is made that the fixed part(iii) example has a zero display.

actual_hypotheses: Exact refers to the analytical identity; machine approximation may differ.
The statement does not require every numerical evaluation to have nonzero error.
claims.correspondence_assessment: The existing real count identity remains exact. The new same-process example exhibits a positive true expectation and a zero rounded evaluation. Terminology and implementation advice receive no extra mathematical clause count.
